title: Conforming Alternate Versions & Page Variations
wcag22Concept: WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.2 permitted non-accessible web pages if an accessible 'Conforming Alternate Version' (a secondary accessible page with identical information and functionality) was provided.
plainEnglishSummary: In WCAG 2.2, developers could achieve conformance under Requirement 5.2.2 by providing a qualifying alternate version of a non-accessible page. WCAG 3 proposals eliminate secondary fallback pages, requiring the primary digital product itself to be natively accessible across user variations.
workingGroupDebate: W3C AGWG members broadly agree that alternate versions lead to stale, poorly maintained secondary experiences that stigmatize disabled users. Current W3C discussions focus on page variations (e.g. responsive breakpoints) rather than allowing separate fallback pages.

debateLinks.title: W3C WCAG 3 GitHub Discussion #623: Conforming Alternate Versions in WCAG 3

personaImpact.designer: Design primary UI components to be natively accessible. Do not rely on 'text-only' toggles.
personaImpact.developer: Build a single, inclusive codebase. Avoid routing screen reader users to a separate accessible domain.
personaImpact.qa: Audit the main user flow. Alternate version pages no longer grant conformance.
personaImpact.productManager: Budget for primary product accessibility rather than secondary fallback maintenance.

title: Page-by-Page Binary Pass/Fail Conformance
wcag22Concept: WCAG 2.2 evaluates accessibility on a strict page-by-page basis (either a whole URL passes 100% of SCs at Level AA or the entire page fails).
wcag3Status: Replaced by Defined Conformance Scope (with Alternative Scoring Proposal)
plainEnglishSummary: WCAG 2.2 evaluated conformance on a strict page-by-page basis. WCAG 3 replaces single-page reliance with a defined 'conformance scope' (which may span entire products, complete processes, paths, views, or components) where all core requirements must be satisfied. An alternative continuous task-scoring model is also being explored by the working group.
workingGroupDebate: Discussions focus on defining clear boundaries for limited scopes (like components and user processes) so that critical tasks cannot be blocked by severe friction, while exploring whether progress is better captured through reporting tiers or percentage scoring.

title: Strict A / AA / AAA Conformance Levels
wcag22Concept: WCAG 2.2 categorizes all criteria into rigid buckets: Level A (minimum), Level AA (standard target for legal compliance), and Level AAA (enhanced).
wcag3Status: Replaced by Single Core Conformance Bar & 6 Reporting Tiers
plainEnglishSummary: The traditional A/AA/AAA tier structure from WCAG 2.x is omitted in WCAG 3. Instead, WCAG 3 defines a single conformance threshold (Tier 3: Conformance) requiring all core requirements to be satisfied, framed by six reporting tiers that express progress toward conformance (Tiers 1–2) and achievements beyond it (Tiers 4–6: Bronze, Silver, Gold).
workingGroupDebate: The working group moved leveling from conformance to reporting in late 2026 drafts (PRs #826, #834), making Bronze an achievement tier above conformance rather than a baseline. A parallel alternative proposal exploring scoring toward conformance followed by Bronze/Silver/Gold awards remains open for public comment.

title: Page-Level 'Accessibility Supported' Reliance
wcag22Concept: WCAG 2.2 allowed authors to rely on specific user agent/assistive technology combinations defined in an author-specified 'accessibility supported' baseline.
wcag3Status: Standardized into Defined Accessibility Support Sets
plainEnglishSummary: In WCAG 2.2, authors relied on subjective, author-defined 'accessibility supported' baselines. WCAG 3 standardizes this by defining two explicit Accessibility Support Sets: a Default set (common browsers/AT supporting English content) and Alternative sets (for other languages, regions, or closed environments), which must be explicitly declared in conformance claims.
workingGroupDebate: The AG Working Group commits to ensuring core requirements have at least one method working with the default accessibility support set at publication time. Current discussions address defining the default set, guidance for creating alternative sets, and handling long-standing AT/UA bugs.
